/api/projects/1.title: The Inuit Knew Where Franklin's Lost Ships Were. No One Listened

idea.title: The Inuit Knew Where Franklin's Lost Ships Were. No One Listened
idea.hook: In 1854, a Scottish doctor named John Rae came home from the Arctic with a silver fork bearing Sir John Franklin's family crest, and a story from the Inuit that Victorian England flatly refused to believe.
idea.why_it_works: Most Franklin videos stop at "129 men vanished." This one starts from a newer question: why did it take 170 years to find ships whose location Inuit witnesses had been describing all along? The video builds from Charles Dickens publicly attacking Rae and the Inuit, through dozens of failed searches, to the payoff: Inuit historian Louie Kamookak's oral-history research helping point searchers to HMS Erebus in 2014, and Inuk ranger Sammy Kogvik's memory of a mast sticking out of the sea ice leading straight to HMS Terror in 2016. The cannibalism evidence should be mentioned once, briefly and respectfully, and never shown.
idea.era: 1845–1859 (the expedition and the early searches), with the payoff in 2014–2016 (the wrecks found) and a 2024 epilogue (James Fitzjames identified through DNA)
idea.documentation: This is a real story with very strong sources: Rae's 1854 Admiralty report and Dickens's essays in Household Words, McClintock's 1859 recovery of the Victory Point note, Parks Canada's records of the 2014 Erebus and 2016 Terror finds, and Dorothy Harley Eber's and Louie Kamookak's published collections of Inuit oral testimony. Check names and dates for the 2014–2016 searches against Parks Canada and Arctic Research Foundation material before scripting.

/api/projects/1/research.content:
## Summary
In 1845 Sir John Franklin took HMS *Erebus* and HMS *Terror* and 129 men into the Canadian Arctic to look for the Northwest Passage. None of them came home. In 1854 John Rae, an Orkney-born doctor working for the Hudson's Bay Company, brought back relics he had bought from Inuit, including a silver fork with Franklin's crest. He also brought their account that the last survivors had starved and turned to cannibalism. Lady Jane Franklin and Charles Dickens attacked the account and the Inuit who gave it. A note found in 1859 confirmed the timeline, and scientific work since the 1990s has confirmed the cannibalism. Inuit testimony collected over 160 years was later used to help find *Erebus* in 2014. An Inuk Ranger's memory led straight to *Terror* in 2016.

## Timeline
- **19 May 1845**: *Erebus* and *Terror* leave Greenhithe on the Thames. About 134 men sail. Five are sent home from Greenland, which leaves 129.
- **Late July 1845**: Whalers see the ships in Baffin Bay. Nobody outside the expedition ever sees them again. (Sources give dates from 26 to 31 July.)
- **Winter 1845–46**: The expedition winters at Beechey Island, where three men die and are buried. Searchers find the graves on 27 August 1850.
- **12 Sept 1846**: The ships become stuck in the ice off northwest King William Island.
- **28 May 1847**: Gore and Des Voeux leave a note in a cairn that ends "All well."
- **11 June 1847**: Sir John Franklin dies.
- **22 April 1848**: The crews abandon the ships. O…

/api/projects/1/script.text:
Picture this. London, autumn of eighteen fifty-four. A Scottish doctor named John Rae opens a bundle of Arctic relics and lifts out a small silver fork. On the back of the handle is a family crest. It belongs to Sir John Franklin, the famous explorer who sailed into the Arctic nine years earlier with two ships and one hundred and twenty-nine men, and was never seen again. Rae didn't find that fork in the snow. He bought it from Inuit hunters. And they told him a story that Victorian England flatly refused to believe.

Here's the strange part. Those ships stayed lost for nearly one hundred and seventy years, even though the Inuit had been describing what happened, and roughly where, the whole time. So why did it take so long? To answer that, we have to go back to the beginning.

On May nineteenth, eighteen forty-five, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror sailed down the River Thames. Their mission was to find the Northwest Passage, a sea route over the top of North America. They were two sturdy ships, packed with supplies and led by one of Britain's most celebrated explorers. In late July, whalers in Baffin Bay spotted them. After that, nobody outside the expedition ever saw them again.

Years passed with no word. Britain sent ship after ship to search. Franklin's wife, Lady Jane Franklin, pushed harder than anyone. Searchers found three graves on tiny Beechey Island, where the crews had spent their first winter. But the ships, and the men who sailed them, were simply gone.

make it interesting and something that will be captivating for viewers

/api/projects/1/script/chat.content: Can we change the script to make it flow better. Make it something that would be easy for a middle schooler to understand

I've rewritten the harder parts so a middle schooler can follow along and the story moves more smoothly. All the facts and the order of events stay the same. Here's what changed:

- **Hard words are now plain words.** "Relics," "informants," "testimony," "folklore" and "archive" have been swapped for simple language. "Admiralty chart" is now "Navy map," and "operations director" is now "the man in charge of the trip."
- **Quick explanations where kids might get stuck:**
  - who the Inuit are
  - what "Inuk" means
  - why the Northwest Passage mattered
  - what The Times was
  - what Rae's phrase "driven to the last resource" meant, said gently
  - what Dickens's word "covetous" means
- **Fixed things that sound confusing out loud.** "Ten thousand pound reward" could sound like a weight, so it's now "ten thousand pounds in prize money." Schwatka's distance now gives miles as well as kilometers. I also took out the repeated "Rae fought back. Rae had…"
- **Smoother flow:** a few small transitions, and shorter sentences in the busier paragraphs.

The script is about 60 words longer, which adds roughly 20 seconds of narration.

edits.find: He'd bought it from Inuit hunters, and they'd told him a story along with it.
edits.replace: He'd bought it from Inuit hunters, the people who have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. And they'd told him a story along with it.

edits.find: England refused to believe that story. For the next hundred and sixty years Franklin's two ships stayed lost, even though Inuit witnesses kept describing where they were. So why did so few people listen?
edits.replace: England refused to believe that story. And for the next hundred and sixty years, Franklin's two ships stayed lost, even though Inuit families kept telling people where they were. So why did almost nobody listen?

edits.find: Their mission was to find the Northwest Passage, the frozen shortcut over the top of North America.
edits.replace: Their mission was to find the Northwest Passage, a sea route through the frozen islands at the top of North America. Whoever found it would have a shortcut from Europe to Asia.

edits.find: At Pelly Bay he met an Inuk hunter named In-nook-poo-zhee-jook. Rae noticed something on the man's cap. It was a band from a Royal Navy officer's cap.
edits.replace: At Pelly Bay he met an Inuk hunter, which means one Inuit man, named In-nook-poo-zhee-jook. Rae noticed something strange on the man's cap. It was a band taken from a Royal Navy officer's cap.

edits.find: Rae followed the trail of stories. Other Inuit traded him relics: forks and spoons marked with officers' initials, including those of Captain Francis Crozier, who commanded Terror. And Franklin's fork.
edits.replace: Rae followed the stories from camp to camp. Other Inuit traded him objects from the lost ships. There were forks and spoons marked with officers' initials, including those of Captain Francis Crozier, the captain of Terror. And, of course, Franklin's fork.
edits.reason: Replace 'relics', remove colon list, simpler wording

edits.find: Rae's informants hadn't seen the place themselves. They were passing on what others had told them.
edits.replace: The people talking to Rae hadn't seen the place themselves. They were passing on what other hunters had told them.

edits.find: Then Rae wrote the line that would wreck his reputation. From the state of the bodies, he reported, the starving men had been "driven to the last resource." Cannibalism.
edits.replace: Then Rae wrote the line that would ruin his good name. From what the Inuit described, he reported, the starving men had been "driven to the last resource." In plain words, some of them had eaten the dead to stay alive.
edits.reason: Explain the old phrase gently for young viewers

edits.find: Rae's report ran in The Times. Lady Franklin was horrified. She rejected it and criticized Rae.
edits.replace: Rae's report was printed in The Times, one of London's biggest newspapers. Lady Franklin was horrified. She refused to believe it and turned against Rae.
edits.reason: Simpler wording, context for The Times

edits.find: Dickens argued that the story was highly improbable and that British sailors would never sink so low.
edits.replace: Dickens argued that the story was almost impossible, and that British sailors would never do such a thing.

edits.find: He wrote, "We believe every savage to be in his heart covetous, treacherous and cruel." He called their testimony "the vague babble of savages."
edits.replace: He wrote, "We believe every savage to be in his heart covetous, treacherous and cruel." In other words, greedy, sneaky and cruel. He called what the Inuit said "the vague babble of savages."
edits.reason: Explain hard words in the quote

edits.find: Rae fought back. Rae had already written in his report that there was no reason to think the Inuit had used any violence, and in late December Household Words printed his reply defending them. He received the ten thousand pound reward for learning the expedition's fate. But unlike other famous Arctic explorers of his day, he was never knighted. No document says why.
edits.replace: Rae fought back. In his report, he had already said there was no reason to think the Inuit had hurt anyone. And in late December, Dickens's own magazine printed Rae's reply defending them. Rae did collect ten thousand pounds in prize money for finding out what happened to the expedition. But unlike other famous Arctic explorers of his day, he was never made a knight. No record explains why.
edits.reason: Remove repetition, avoid 'pound' sounding like weight, simpler wording

prompts.prompt: Hunter pointing. Over-the-shoulder shot from behind a stick figure with a fur-trimmed parka hood, pointing a mittened hand toward a specific stretch of icy coastline and low rocky islands in the distance, a stone cairn nearby. Clear, confident pose. Minimalist stick figure illustration, clean hand-drawn style: bold black outlines, round white heads with simple expressive faces (dot eyes, eyebrows, line mouth), thin black stick arms and legs that show as plain black lines wherever clothing does not cover them, with sleeves and trousers drawn as flat colored clothing over them, and simple round cartoon hands that are always the same color as the head, never black, unless a character's look gives gloves or mittens, flat colors for props, clothing and backgrounds (icy steel blue, navy blue, parchment tan, deep crimson, mustard gold, slate gray). The background fills the whole frame and matches the scene's place, time of day and lighting: night scenes are dark, indoor scenes show the room, never a blank white or paper background. Uncluttered composition with one clear focal point, 16:9 widescreen. No text, no letters, no numbers, no captions, no speech bubbles, no watermark.

slots.beat_text: Picture this. London, autumn of eighteen fifty-four.
A Scottish doctor named John Rae opens a bundle of Arctic relics and lifts out a small silver fork.
On the back of the handle is a family crest.
It belongs to Sir John Franklin, the famous explorer
who sailed into the Arctic nine years earlier with two ships and one hundred and twenty-nine men,
and was never seen again.
Rae didn't find that fork in the snow. He bought it from Inuit hunters.
And they told him a story that Victorian England flatly refused to believe.
Here's the strange part.
Those ships stayed lost for nearly one hundred and seventy years,
even though the Inuit had been describing what happened,
and roughly where, the whole time.
John Rae wasn't even looking for Franklin.
In the spring of eighteen fifty-four, he was mapping coastline for the Hudson's Bay Company.
Rae traveled the way the Inuit did.
He hunted for his food,
built snow houses,
and moved fast and light.
At Pelly Bay, he met an Inuk hunter named In-nook-poo-zhee-jook.
The man had something that didn't belong in the Arctic:
a cap band from a Royal Navy uniform.
Rae asked where it came from.
The hunter said that some winters back,
other Inuit had seen about forty white men dragging a boat south over the ice.
He also wrote that there was no reason to think the Inuit had harmed anyone.
He carried his report and the relics home to London,
thinking he was delivering the answer to the greatest mystery of his age.
And that's when everything went wrong.
The report ran in The Times,
and Victorian England recoiled.
British naval heroes, driven to that? Unthinkable.
Lady Franklin rejected it outright.
Then the most famous writer in the country stepped in.
That December, Charles Dickens published a two-part essay in his magazine, Household Words.
He argued Rae's account was highly improbable.
He even suggested that if anyone had done something terrible, it may have been the Inuit.
The first note, from eighteen forty-seven, ended with two words: All well.
But squeezed into the margin was a second message, from April eighteen forty-eight.
Franklin was dead.
The ships had been trapped in ice for over a year and a half.
One hundred and five survivors were abandoning them to walk south.
Walking south was exactly what the Inuit had described.
Nearby, searchers found a boat holding the remains of two men,
along with books, soap, combs, and about forty pounds of chocolate.
Every new clue matched the Inuit account.
So now you might be wondering:
if the Inuit were right about the men, were they right about the ships too?
They were. And that's where this story gets truly frustrating.
He later said something like this:
without that testimony, searchers wouldn't know where to look.
In the town of Gjoa Haven,
a teacher named Louie Kamookak spent years gathering stories from elders and matching them against explorers' journals.
He pointed out something outsiders kept missing.
You couldn't ask the elders about Franklin, because they didn't know the name.
You had to ask about the ships,
and the strangers,
and what their families remembered.
Even then, it wasn't easy.
The accounts pointed to more than one possible site.
Parks Canada searched year after year starting in two thousand eight.
A week later, Canada's Prime Minister announced it to the world.
That same month, a memorial stone to John Rae was placed in Westminster Abbey,
just below the memorial to Franklin.
It came one hundred and sixty years after Rae brought home the truth.
But Terror was still missing,
and the man who would find it almost wasn't on the boat.
He was Sammy Kogvik, a Canadian Ranger from Gjoa Haven.
As Kogvik told reporters, around two thousand nine he was out on the ice in Terror Bay
when he saw a wooden pole sticking up through it.
He posed beside it for a photo.
Then, on the way home, he lost the camera.
In twenty sixteen, Kogvik joined the research ship Martin Bergmann as a last-minute replacement.
The Inuit had told the truth.
So why did it take nearly one hundred and seventy years?
The answer wasn't hidden in the ice.
It was kept in the memories of the people who had been there all along.
A handful of outsiders listened,
but far too many didn't.
Charles Dickens called it babble.
It turned out to be the best map anyone ever had.
If you like stories where the overlooked witness turns out to be right, subscribe. There are more coming.

titles: The Inuit Knew Where Franklin's Lost Ships Were. No One Listened
Charles Dickens Called It 'Babble.' It Was the Best Map Ever
How Inuit Memory Found Two Ships Lost for Nearly 170 Years
A Silver Fork, a Vanished Crew, and a Truth Britain Rejected
The Arctic Mystery Victorian England Refused to Solve
/api/projects/1/publish.description:
In 1854, a doctor came home from the Arctic with Sir John Franklin's silver fork and the Inuit account of what happened to his 129 lost men. Victorian England refused to believe it. Charles Dickens himself dismissed the Inuit testimony as "babble."

The ships HMS Erebus and HMS Terror stayed lost for nearly 170 years, even though Inuit witnesses had described what happened, and roughly where, the whole time. This is the story of John Rae, the note found under a pile of stones, the testimony that sat forgotten in old notebooks, and the people who finally went back and listened.

This video is narrated with an AI voice and illustrated with stick-figure art.

6:39 The Ranger's Story
